rules.title: ITAR "U.S. Person" Definition
rules.summary: Under ITAR (22 CFR 120.62), a "U.S. person" is a U.S. citizen, a lawful permanent resident (green card holder), or a "protected individual" under 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) (which also covers certain asylees/refugees who timely pursue naturalization). Anyone else — including H-1B, L-1, O-1, F-1/OPT, J-1, and TN visa holders — is a "foreign person" under 22 CFR 120.63, no matter how long they've lived or worked in the U.S. Most defense-tech roles touching USML-controlled technical data require the worker to be a U.S. person, or the employer to hold a specific DDTC license/exemption for that individual. This is strictly a citizenship/immigration-status test — it has nothing to do with whether someone already holds a security clearance, which is a separate question (see dcsa-timeliness) with its own, much stricter rule for anyone who is NOT a U.S. person (see laa-non-citizen) — green card holders don't need that stricter rule, since they already qualify as U.S. persons here.
keyPoints: U.S. person = citizen, green card holder (LPR), or certain protected asylees/refugees (8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3))
Does NOT include H-1B, L-1, O-1, F-1/OPT, J-1, TN, or any other non-immigrant visa holder
Green card holders qualify directly as "lawful permanent resident" (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(20)) — no naturalization-timing condition attached to that prong
Asylees/refugees without a green card qualify only if they applied for naturalization within the timeframes 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) requires
A company can still employ foreign persons under a specific DDTC license or exemption, but that's the exception, not the default
This is about ITAR access, not about getting an actual security clearance — someone who is NOT a U.S. person faces a separate, much stricter clearance-eligibility rule (see laa-non-citizen)

rules.title: Limited Access Authorization (LAA) for Non-U.S. Citizens
rules.summary: A Limited Access Authorization (LAA) is a separate, much stricter pathway than ITAR's "U.S. person" test (see itar-us-person) for a non-U.S. citizen to access U.S. classified information, under 32 CFR § 117.10(k). It is capped at SECRET — never TOP SECRET, Restricted Data/Formerly Restricted Data, COMSEC information, intelligence information, or (except for NATO-member nationals under specific conditions) NATO information. A Cognizant Security Agency may only grant one in "rare circumstances": the individual has specialized skills urgently needed for a specific U.S. Government contract AND a cleared or clearable U.S. citizen is not readily available, approved by a Government Contracting Activity senior official — it is not a general clearance and does not transfer between contracts. A green card holder (lawful permanent resident) already qualifies as a U.S. person under ITAR with no special justification needed (see itar-us-person); an LAA pathway is for someone who does NOT qualify as a U.S. person at all.
keyPoints: Capped at SECRET — never TOP SECRET, Restricted Data/Formerly Restricted Data, COMSEC information, intelligence information, or (except NATO-member nationals under specific conditions) NATO information (32 CFR § 117.10(k))
Granted only in "rare circumstances": specialized skills urgently needed for a specific U.S. Government contract, and a cleared or clearable U.S. citizen is not readily available
Requires approval from a Government Contracting Activity senior official — not an automatic or routine determination
Scoped to the specific contract/program that justified it, not a general-purpose clearance

A different, stricter test than ITAR's "U.S. person" status (see itar-us-person) — a green card holder already qualifies as a U.S. person under ITAR with no special justification, while the LAA pathway is for someone who does NOT qualify as a U.S. person at all

rules.title: EAR "Deemed Export" vs. ITAR
rules.summary: Under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR, 15 CFR 734.13), releasing controlled "technology" or source code to a foreign person inside the U.S. is legally treated as an export to that person's country of citizenship or permanent residency — a "deemed export." EAR is administered by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a separate regime from ITAR's DDTC/State Department. Practically, EAR is more graduated than ITAR: it exempts U.S. dual citizens and green card holders outright, and allows case-by-case deemed-export licenses for other foreign nationals depending on their specific nationality and the technology involved. ITAR has no equivalent per-nationality licensing path for most defense articles — it is close to a binary U.S.-person/foreign-person test instead. For an engineering job: if the work touches USML-controlled defense technical data, expect an essentially all-U.S.-persons team; if it's "dual-use" tech controlled only under EAR, a foreign-national teammate may be workable with the right export license.
keyPoints: Deemed export = releasing controlled technology or source code to a foreign person inside the U.S., treated as an export to their home country (15 CFR 734.13(b))
Administered by BIS/Commerce (EAR) — a distinct regime from DDTC/State (ITAR)
EAR explicitly exempts U.S. dual citizens and green card holders from deemed-export treatment
EAR licensing can be nationality-specific and case-by-case; ITAR generally cannot — ITAR is closer to all-or-nothing U.S.-person access
Which regime applies depends on whether the specific technology is on the USML (ITAR) or is dual-use/EAR-only

rules.title: SF-86 and the eApp Filing System
rules.summary: The SF-86 ("Questionnaire for National Security Positions") is the core background-investigation form behind any security clearance, and it is filed electronically, not on paper. The legacy e-QIP filing portal is being phased out in favor of "eApp," and the underlying form itself is also changing: DCSA began an internal rollout of a new, consolidated "Personnel Vetting Questionnaire" (PVQ) in April 2026, intended to eventually replace the SF-86/SF-85/SF-85P forms outright. Only the updated (February 2024 edition) SF-86 filed through eApp has been accepted since mid-2025; older/legacy-form submissions stopped being accepted August 1, 2025. Candidates fill this out themselves once sponsored by an employer — it covers 10+ years of history, foreign contacts, and finances, and should never be filled out by, or shared with, a third party.
keyPoints: SF-86 = the standard background-investigation questionnaire for national security positions
Filed electronically via "eApp," which is replacing the older "e-QIP" portal
Pre-2024 paper/legacy SF-86 versions stopped being accepted August 1, 2025
A further-consolidated "Personnel Vetting Questionnaire" (PVQ) began internal DCSA rollout in April 2026 and is intended to eventually replace SF-86/85/85P
OPM has not proposed content changes to the SF-86 form itself pending this broader replacement

rules.title: NBIS vs. DISS: Current System of Record
rules.summary: DISS (Defense Information System for Security) replaced the older JPAS as the system of record in 2021. The National Background Investigation Services (NBIS) program was meant to eventually replace DISS entirely, but as of November 2026 that full cutover has not happened — DCSA has actually pulled key case-management functions back toward an upgraded DISS. Industry case-initiation and review ("IRA") functionality moved into "DISS-JVS" on July 31, 2026; September 30, 2026 was the last day to start new cases in "NBIS-Agency"; and NBIS-Agency becomes fully read-only after November 30, 2026, with any unfinished case needing to be re-started in DISS-JVS. In short: DISS-JVS, not NBIS, is the live day-to-day system right now. Either way, access to these systems is restricted to vetted Facility Security Officers — individual candidates and recruiters cannot query them directly, which is exactly why self-attestation plus FSO verification at offer stage remain the only legitimate path.
keyPoints: JPAS → DISS transition completed in 2021
NBIS was meant to replace DISS, but as of Nov 2026 that full replacement has not happened
DCSA is moving case-initiation/review functions back into an upgraded "DISS-JVS," not forward into NBIS
Key 2026 dates: DISS-JVS industry go-live July 31; last NBIS-Agency case-initiation Sept 30; NBIS-Agency read-only after Nov 30
Only FSOs can query DISS/NBIS/Scattered Castles — there is no way for a candidate or recruiter to self-verify a clearance in these systems

rules.title: SEAD 4: The 13 Adjudicative Guidelines
rules.summary: Security Executive Agent Directive 4 (signed by the Director of National Intelligence in December 2016, effective June 8, 2017) sets the single, government-wide set of criteria every agency uses to decide whether to grant or keep someone's security clearance eligibility. It defines 13 guidelines, lettered A through M, each evaluated together under a "whole person" concept — no single factor is automatically disqualifying, and every guideline lists both disqualifying and mitigating conditions. No superseding revision of SEAD 4 was found as of this research date; it remains the current, controlling version.
keyPoints: A — Allegiance to the United States
B — Foreign Influence
C — Foreign Preference
D — Sexual Behavior
E — Personal Conduct
F — Financial Considerations
G — Alcohol Consumption
H — Drug Involvement and Substance Misuse
I — Psychological Conditions
J — Criminal Conduct
K — Handling Protected Information
L — Outside Activities
M — Use of Information Technology

rules.title: SEAD 7: Clearance Reciprocity
rules.summary: Security Executive Agent Directive 7 (November 9, 2018) requires federal agencies to accept another authorized agency's existing background investigation and clearance-eligibility determination at the same or higher level, instead of re-investigating someone from scratch, as long as the investigation is still within scope. For industry/contractor employees specifically, this duty is implemented through 32 CFR 117.10 (the NISPOM rule). Reciprocity generally holds as long as the break in federal service or classified access does not exceed 24 months and the underlying investigation is not older than 7 years with no new derogatory information — within those bounds, a reciprocity determination is supposed to be made within about 5 business days. Only the Security Executive Agent (the DNI) may generally disallow reciprocal recognition, and only for specific national-security reasons.
keyPoints: Agencies must accept another authorized agency's clearance eligibility at the same or higher level
Reciprocity generally applies only if the break in access/employment is under 24 months and the investigation is under 7 years old with no new adverse information
A reciprocity determination on a still-valid case is supposed to be made within about 5 business days
For NISP/contractor personnel, reciprocity is implemented via 32 CFR 117.10
Only the Security Executive Agent (DNI) can generally disallow reciprocal recognition, for specific national-security reasons

rules.title: Continuous Vetting (Trusted Workforce 2.0)
rules.summary: Continuous Vetting (CV) replaces the old model of one deep reinvestigation every 5-10 years with ongoing, automated record checks (criminal, terrorism, financial, public records, foreign travel, and more) that generate alerts for a human adjudicator to review as they occur. It is the centerpiece of the government's "Trusted Workforce 2.0" reform. As of the end of June 2026, DCSA formally retired legacy periodic reinvestigations for the national-security workforce (with only limited exceptions), making CV the default; the broader federal "public trust" population is still being enrolled (about 54% as of mid-2026, expected substantially complete by the end of 2026). Day to day, a cleared person generally no longer faces one big reinvestigation case every several years — instead they are expected to self-report qualifying life events between automated checks, and an alert can trigger a review at any time rather than only on a fixed schedule.
keyPoints: Replaces periodic reinvestigation (previously every 5 years for TS/SCI, 5-10 years for Secret) with ongoing automated checks
Legacy periodic reinvestigations for the national-security population were formally retired at the end of June 2026
Automated alerts (financial, criminal, terrorism, travel, public records) are reviewed by adjudicators as they occur, not on a fixed cycle
NISP contractor personnel now get a simplified questionnaire every 5 years instead of a full reinvestigation case (announced May 19, 2026)
Non-sensitive public trust federal population enrollment is still ramping (~54% as of FY2026 Q3)

rules.title: Interim (Temporary) Clearance Eligibility
rules.summary: An interim — officially "temporary" — eligibility determination lets someone start working at the Top Secret, Secret, or Confidential level before their full investigation and final adjudication are complete, based on preliminary checks showing no disqualifying information so far. It does not cover Restricted Data, COMSEC, or NATO classified information, which always require a final determination, and SCI/Special Access Program access on an interim basis is discretionary and decided case by case. Only U.S. citizens can receive temporary eligibility, and by regulation (32 CFR 117.10) it cannot last more than one year without specific extension approval. It is fully revocable if the completed investigation turns up a problem.
keyPoints: Covers Top Secret/Secret/Confidential collateral work only — not RD, COMSEC, or NATO information
SCI/SAP access on an interim basis is case-by-case, not automatic
Only U.S. citizens are eligible for temporary/interim eligibility
Capped at one year by regulation (32 CFR 117.10) absent specific approval to extend
Fully revocable — it is a preliminary determination, not a guarantee

rules.title: Facility Clearance (FCL) Sponsorship for a New Company
rules.summary: A Facility Clearance (FCL) lets a specific company location store, access, or work with classified information, and a company cannot apply for one on its own — it must be sponsored, either by a government contracting activity with a classified contract for that company or by an already-cleared prime contractor that needs to subcontract classified work to it. The sponsor submits a request through DCSA's National Industrial Security System, typically including a DD Form 254 and a sponsorship letter; DCSA's Facility Clearance Branch then reviews it, and if accepted, the company generally has about 20 days to return required paperwork once DCSA's processing clock starts. The government funds DCSA's own FCL processing; the company's real cost is building out compliant security processes and designating a Facility Security Officer (FSO) beforehand. For an early-stage startup with no FCL yet, the first real bottleneck is usually finding a willing sponsor, not DCSA's internal processing — and first-time FCL packages are rejected on their first submission a majority of the time, which routinely adds weeks to months.
keyPoints: A company cannot self-apply for an FCL — it must be sponsored by a government contracting activity or an already-cleared prime contractor
Sponsorship request goes through DCSA's NISS, usually with a DD Form 254 and a sponsorship letter
The company should designate a Facility Security Officer (FSO) before or at sponsorship
No government fee for FCL processing itself — the company's cost is internal compliance and FSO time
Initial/upgrade FCL packages are rejected on first submission a majority of the time (DCSA-cited ~70% rejection rate, ~2.5 submission cycles on average), which adds real time

Industry sources commonly describe a 3-9 month range from sponsorship to a granted FCL for straightforward cases, and 6-18 months where foreign ownership/control/influence (FOCI) mitigation is involved; DCSA itself declines to commit to a fixed timeline

rules.title: Current DCSA Clearance Timeliness (FY2026 Q3)
rules.summary: DCSA's own FY2026 Q3 industry figures, presented at the September 2, 2026 NISPPAC public meeting, show an initial Top Secret clearance for industry averaging 243 days end-to-end (20 days initiation + 97 days investigation + 126 days adjudication), and an initial Secret clearance averaging 197 days end-to-end (21 + 59 + 117). These figures have moved a great deal over the past two years: the investigation phase itself has gotten much faster (Top Secret investigation time fell from 234 days a year earlier to 97 days), but the adjudication phase has gotten slower by nearly as much (40 to 126 days for Top Secret over the same period), so total end-to-end time has not improved much and ticked back up this quarter. A separate, government-wide (not industry-specific) measure from the Performance Accountability Council shows the investigation phase alone averaging 61 days for Secret-tier and 82 days for Top-Secret-tier cases in the same quarter, consistent with the industry figures once the investigation step is isolated.
keyPoints: Initial TS (industry), FY2026 Q3: ~243 days end-to-end (20 initiate + 97 investigate + 126 adjudicate)
Initial Secret (industry), FY2026 Q3: ~197 days end-to-end (21 initiate + 59 investigate + 117 adjudicate)
Investigation time has dropped sharply since FY2024-2025; adjudication time has risen just as sharply — that is the current bottleneck
These are DCSA's own published figures (NISPPAC meeting, Sept. 2026), not a stale historical estimate
Figures move quarter to quarter; treat as a snapshot and check for a newer NISPPAC/DCSA release before relying on them long-term

rules.title: Zero-Knowledge Passport Proofs (Self, zkPassport)
rules.summary: Self Protocol and zkPassport are open-source systems that let someone scan their passport, national ID, or similar chip-based document with their phone and generate a zero-knowledge proof of a specific fact — like being over 18, a citizen of a given country, a unique human, or not on a sanctions list — without revealing the underlying document or any other personal data. Both generate the proof on the user's own device and explicitly avoid storing documents or raw data centrally. These are general-purpose identity/humanity tools (built for things like KYC, Sybil-resistant distribution, and age verification) — they have no connection to the U.S. personnel-security-clearance system and cannot prove, and do not claim to prove, that someone holds any level of security clearance.
keyPoints: Both generate zero-knowledge proofs client-side from an NFC passport/ID chip scan
Can prove: age threshold, nationality/citizenship, personhood/uniqueness, sanctions-list status, document validity
Cannot prove, and are not designed to prove, security clearance status or classified-access eligibility
No integration with DISS, NBIS, Scattered Castles, or any DCSA system
The closest thing to a real-world analogy for a future "prove a fact without showing the document" clearance credential — but no such clearance credential exists today

rules.title: W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0 and SD-JWT
rules.summary: W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0 became an official, finished W3C Recommendation on May 15, 2025 — the standard web format for cryptographically-signed, tamper-evident digital credentials (comparable to a digital diploma or ID card). It deliberately supports multiple ways of cryptographically "securing" a credential, including SD-JWT. SD-JWT itself (the selective-disclosure mechanism that lets a holder reveal only some fields of a credential) was finalized by the IETF as RFC 9901 in November 2025. A richer profile built on it, "SD-JWT VC," is further along in standardization (draft revision -22 as of October 2026, in IESG review) but is not yet a final RFC. A VC 2.1 maintenance update is already in early draft (April 2026) under a new 2026-2028 working group charter. None of this is specific to clearances — it is general infrastructure for any digital credential.
keyPoints: VC Data Model 2.0 = W3C Recommendation (finished standard) since May 15, 2025
VC 2.0 supports multiple credential-securing mechanisms, including SD-JWT, not just one
Base SD-JWT mechanism = finalized as RFC 9901 (IETF, November 2025)
SD-JWT VC (the verifiable-credential profile) is still an in-progress IETF draft (rev. -22, Oct. 2026), not yet a final RFC
A VC 2.1 maintenance revision is already in First Public Working Draft (April 2026)

rules.title: Mobile Driver's License (mDL) / ISO 18013-5
rules.summary: ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 is the international standard defining how a phone-based mobile driver's license works and how it is presented to a verifier (for example, at an airport security checkpoint); it was approved in August 2021 and remains the currently-published edition, though a second edition is already in development (committee-draft stage as of 2026, not yet published). In the U.S., AAMVA layers additional implementation guidance on top of it for state DMV mDL programs, several states (including California, Colorado, Arizona, and Maryland) have live mDL programs built on it, and TSA's CAT-2 readers at 250+ airport checkpoints already accept an 18013-5-compliant mDL. Like the zero-knowledge passport tools above, this proves identity/age-type facts from a state-issued credential — it has no relationship to security clearance status.
keyPoints: ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021 defines the mDL data model and verifier-presentation protocol; approved August 2021
A companion standard, ISO/IEC 18013-7, covering remote/online presentation, was published in 2024
A second edition of 18013-5 is in development (committee-draft stage) but not yet published
AAMVA adds U.S.-specific implementation guidance for state DMV programs
TSA's CAT-2 readers already accept 18013-5-compliant mDLs at 250+ U.S. airport checkpoints
Proves identity/age facts from a driver's-license-grade credential — unrelated to clearance status
